levels.title: Find the Steps
levels.story: Ranger Rowan hands Kit a lantern with no oil and points up the hill. "Light it before dark," says Rowan. "There are a dozen things you could do first, and only a few orders that work." Kit sits on a stump and starts a list.

everyday.scene: A phone's walking directions say 'turn left, then take the second right, then cross at the lights'. Somebody, or something, worked out those moves in order before you took a single step.
everyday.question: What does it mean to make a plan?
everyday.answer: To plan is to choose a list of actions, in the right order, that takes you from where you are to where you want to be, before you act.

lessons.title: Start, goal and actions
text: A planning problem has three parts. The initial state says how the world is now. The goal says what must be true at the end. The actions are the moves you are allowed, and each one changes the world a little.
A plan is a list of actions which, started from the initial state, ends in a state where the goal is true. Kit's lantern is empty, the oil is in the shed, and the goal is a lit lantern.

terms.meaning: How the world is at the start.
What must be true when the plan is finished.
One allowed move that changes the world.
A list of actions that gets you from the start to the goal.

head: Part
In Kit's lantern problem
rows: Kit in the cabin, oil in the shed, lantern empty
Walk to the shed, pick up the oil, walk back, pour it in, light it

lessons.title: Order matters
text: Each action only works when its conditions hold. Kit cannot pour oil before fetching it, and cannot light a dry lantern. So a plan is a sequence, not a pile of actions.

The number of possible orders grows fast. Three chores can be done in 6 orders, five chores in 120, and ten chores in 3,628,800. Most orders fail somewhere, so a program needs a clever way to search rather than trying every order.

predict.prompt: How many different orders can 4 chores be done in?

deeper.title: Counting orders
text: For n different chores the number of orders is n x (n - 1) x ... x 2 x 1, written n!. That is the number of ways to line them up.

lessons.title: What a planner assumes
text: The simplest kind of planning is called classical planning. It makes friendly assumptions: you know exactly where you start, every action has one predictable result, actions take no time and happen one at a time, and there is a single agent.
Real life bends these rules. A match can fail to light, or a neighbour can move the can. Planners start with the simple case because its ideas carry over to harder ones.

deeper.title: Beyond classical
text: Other kinds of planning allow actions that might fail, a world you can only partly see, actions that take time, or several agents. This game stays with classical planning.

steps.say: The start: Kit is in the cabin, the oil can is in the shed, and the lantern in the cabin is empty. The goal: a lit lantern.
Action 1: walk to the shed. Kit's place changes. Nothing else does.
Action 2: pick up the oil can. This works because Kit is in the same place as the can.

predict.prompt: Kit is in the shed holding the oil. Could Kit fill the lantern right now?

options.text: No, the lantern is in the cabin and Kit is not
No, the oil can is empty

hints: An action only works when its conditions are true.
Pouring needs Kit and the lantern in the same place.

steps.say: Action 3: walk back to the cabin, carrying the oil.
Action 4: pour the oil into the lantern. Two things change at once: the can is used up and the lantern is full.
Action 5: strike a match and light the lantern. The goal is true. These five actions, in this order, are a plan.

options.text: No: a dry lantern will not light, so the oil must go in first
Yes, if Kit strikes two matches
No, because the shed is closed

hints: Think about what the lantern needs before it can burn.
An action's conditions must already be true.

fieldNotes.title: Planning problems
fieldNotes.text: Given a description of the starting situation, the goal, and the available actions, the planning problem is to find a plan that reaches the goal.

fieldNotes.title: Classical planning
fieldNotes.text: The simplest planning problem has one known starting state, actions with no duration and predictable results, one action at a time, and a single agent.

fieldNotes.title: Route directions
fieldNotes.text: In classical planning, a plan is a sequence of actions, because it is known in advance which actions will be needed. A list of turns to reach a place is a plan in that sense.

summary: You met the three parts of a planning problem, saw that order matters, counted how fast the orders grow, and learned the friendly rules of classical planning.
Rowan holds up the lit lantern. "Five steps, in order." Kit tucks the list into the notebook. "Next: how to find the list when I do not know it."

mistake.title: Thinking order does not matter
mistake.text: Actions depend on one another. Doing them in the wrong order means a condition is false when you need it, so the plan breaks.
